_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies". A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn. "cue" is when the talk comes on: "start" as the lesson opens, {"after": "<figure>"} once that figure's task is done, or "check" as the final check opens. "locals" names who in town asked a forecast question, by the forecast's "id" in the lesson file.

turns.them: W7HAR, W7HAR, this is W7DQ, Walla Walla. Fifteen years, and the same old crackle. Are you still up there, Harrow?

replies.back: Older is the only direction anybody goes. I’ve gone a fair way down it myself.
They took our sets off the air for the war. I retired from the radio, not from the weather. Now we’re back on, and so am I.

turns.them: Have you seen the papers? A fellow at General Electric back East, Schaefer, flew over a mountain in Massachusetts ten days ago, dropped dry ice on a cloud, and made it snow. On purpose.

replies.back: That’s why I’m calling. Half the county has read it, and Mabel has read it to the other half.

replies.say: Sounds like the rainmakers at the county fair.
replies.back: That’s what I said. Then I read the report. This one is real physics. Mostly.

turns.them: And your Hap Delaney came home from the war with a surplus crop duster and a head full of ideas. He has already priced dry ice from the ice house in Spokane.

replies.say: Hap with a duster. Heaven help the sky.
replies.back: Heaven may have to. You’ll have to help it first.

replies.say: Then we’d better learn how it works.
replies.back: Good. There’s a new workbook on the train. Same as before: read it, and bring me the questions.

turns.them: So you’ve made it snow in a box. At −3 °C, which one works?

replies.back: By sheer cold. Silver iodide doesn’t wake up until about −5.
Not yet at −3. It wants about −5 or colder. Dry ice works at any temperature below freezing.
Dry ice does. It makes its own ice by sheer cold.

turns.them: Schaefer’s box was an ordinary home freezer lined with black velvet. Don’t tell Edna. She’ll want to know what became of the velvet.

replies.back: Fifteen years, and she still has the receipt for that tablecloth.
The box is simple. The flying is not.

turns.them: Hap asked me straight out: more dry ice is better, isn’t it?

replies.say: No. Too much and the crystals stay too small to fall.
replies.back: Overseeded: all that ice and not a flake on the ground. Tell him a pound a mile, give or take.
Overseed it and each crystal gets a crumb of water and never grows big enough to fall. About a pound a mile does it.
It matters a great deal. Too little gives flurries, too much gives a veil of ice. About a pound a mile.

turns.them: He’ll want to try it on the next grey deck that settles over the basin. Rime on the fences is your sign that it’s supercooled.

replies.back: Then he can save the dry ice for the ice cream social.

turns.them: Photographs first, the same as ever. Then Hap and Dutch have questions. Hap’s are louder.

replies.back: Dutch Kessler always has questions. He just asks them slowly.
